title: Duplicate-Blind "At-Least-Once" Message Consumer
pattern: An event stream or message queue handler function that modifies state or triggers side-effects directly based on the received payload, without performing a check against a local transaction/idempotency log or sequence record.
why_bad: Real-world message brokers (e.g., RabbitMQ, Kafka, SQS) provide at-least-once delivery semantics [38, 234]. Due to consumer crashes, transient network drops, or dropped ACKs, the broker regularly redelivers messages [198, 234, 235]. If the consumer does not explicitly deduplicate incoming events, duplicate delivery results in duplicate processing, permanently corrupting database values, inflating logs, and triggering duplicate side-effects (e.g., double billing) [113, 235, 236].
detection: Identify functions mapped as message listeners or event consumers (e.g., handling parameters like `KafkaMessage`, `SqsMessage`, `Event`) that execute write queries or side-effects (e.g., payments, email triggers) but lack any intermediate logic querying a unique message identifier against an idempotency database or log.
fix: Implement an idempotent receiver pattern by logging every processed message's unique ID in a local persistent storage table in an atomic transaction alongside the business state update, discarding any subsequent deliveries [33, 221, 237].
source: Vaughn Vernon, *Implementing Domain-Driven Design*, Chapter 8 (Event De-duplication) / passages [221, 222, 234, 235, 237]; Alex Petrov, *Database Internals*, Chapter 8 / passages [32, 33]; Martin Kleppmann, *Designing Data-Intensive Applications*, Chapter 11 / passages [113, 198, 209].
